findings.claim: “The five primitive data types are: integer, real, Boolean, char, and string” (repeated at n2, n17 and in the conclusion, plus the n3 revision tip).
findings.truth: The specification names FOUR primitive data types (integer, real, Boolean, char) and lists string with array and record as one- and two-dimensional STRUCTURED data types. Teaching string as a primitive would cost a mark on any question that asks a student to name the primitive types or to pick out a structured type.
findings.evidence: specs/edexcel/computer-science-1CP1.md 6.3.1 — “primitive data types (integer, real, Boolean, char) and one- and two-dimensional structured data types (string, array, record)”

findings.claim: “Examiners award marks for meaningful identifiers when you write code — single-letter names (except conventional loop counters such as i) will cost marks.”
findings.truth: Invented examiner behaviour. The specification lists meaningful identifiers as one of five readability techniques; no published rule says single-letter names lose marks. State the requirement, not a mark-scheme claim.

findings.claim: “Examiners penalise vague answers such as ‘it holds text.’”
findings.truth: Fabricated examiner claim. The point (a char holds one character, a string holds a sequence) stands on its own without asserting what examiners do.
findings.evidence: house rule on fabricated examiner claims; nothing in the spec supports it

findings.claim: “Python supports six arithmetic operators.” The same sentence then lists seven: + - * / // % and **.
findings.truth: Seven. The specification names addition, subtraction, division, multiplication, modulus, integer division and exponentiation. The count contradicts the list in its own sentence, so a student revising “six operators” may drop ** from a list answer.
findings.evidence: specs/edexcel/computer-science-1CP1.md 6.5.1; recount of the sentence itself

findings.claim: KC 1: “A list called marks has 6 elements. What is the index of the last element?” Options are 6 / 5 / -1 / 4; only 5 is marked correct.
findings.truth: -1 is also a correct index of the last element in Python, and this very lesson teaches that (“Negative indices count from the end: scores[-1] is the last element”). A student who follows the lesson can be marked wrong. Replace the -1 distractor with 0.
findings.evidence: lesson 4 content n6; recomputation in Python 3

findings.claim: “the postcode must be between 6 and 8 characters … A basic pattern check might verify: no spaces, at least 6 characters” — while the code immediately below tests len(code) < 5 or len(code) > 7.
findings.truth: The code is right and the prose is wrong. With the space removed a UK postcode is 5 to 7 characters (outward part 2 to 4, inward part always 3), so the code accepts 5 to 7. A student who trusts the prose gets a different result from the program when tracing it, and would write the wrong bounds in a pattern-check answer.
findings.evidence: recomputation in Python 3: is_valid_postcode('SW1A1AA') is True (7 characters), 'AB12CD' is True (6); UK postcode format — outward 2 to 4 characters, inward always 3

findings.claim: A pattern check “is the fourth validation type and is unique to this specification”.
findings.truth: It is not unique to this board. A pattern (format) check is a standard validation type taught on other GCSE computer science specifications too. It is simply the fourth of the four checks this specification names.

findings.claim: “A programme may need both: validate the password format first …”
findings.truth: In British English a computer program is spelt “program”. “Programme” means a broadcast or a schedule. Every other use in this unit is “program”.
findings.evidence: British spelling convention; the rest of the unit

findings.claim: “Always use the with keyword — it automatically closes the file and earns marks in ‘Write’ questions.”
findings.truth: Fabricated mark claim. The with statement is a convenience, not a requirement, and the unit never gives the student the alternative. Say what with does and give the close() call that is needed without it.
findings.evidence: specs/edexcel/computer-science-1CP1.md 6.4.2 (read from and write to comma separated value text files); no mark-scheme source

findings.claim: “Edexcel is precise about the distinction — confusing them is one of the most penalised errors in exam answers.”
findings.truth: Invented examiner statistic. The distinction between a function and a procedure is real (6.6.2) but no source supports “one of the most penalised errors”.

findings.claim: “Writing ‘a function performs a task’ without mentioning the return value is an incomplete definition that loses marks.”
findings.truth: The definition really is incomplete, but the mark consequence is invented. Drop the mark claim and keep the point.
findings.evidence: house rule on fabricated mark-scheme claims

findings.claim: “The most common mark loss in ‘Write a Subprogram’ questions is …” and “‘A mistake in the code’ is too vague for marks.”
findings.truth: Both assert mark-scheme behaviour with no source. The advice itself is sound, so reword it as advice.
findings.evidence: house rule on fabricated examiner claims

findings.claim: Every lesson's practice bank is written as written-paper items — “4 marks — Explain”, “6 marks — Discuss”, “2 marks — Define” — with prose mark schemes (for example lesson 5 question 6, “Discuss the limitations of validation”, 6 marks). This pattern runs through all six lessons.
findings.truth: Topic 6 is assessed ONLY on Paper 2, which is a 2-hour onscreen examination of 75 marks with six compulsory questions, answered in an IDE using Python 3 with Pearson-supplied coding files. Topic 6 never appears on the written paper, which assesses Topics 1 to 5. So these command words match no paper the student will sit. Options: (a) leave them, because they rehearse the underlying knowledge and are good revision; (b) relabel the tariff line as revision practice rather than exam-style; (c) rebuild the bank as code-writing and code-amending tasks. Recommendation: (b) now, and (c) only if the unit is rebuilt. No edit written.
findings.evidence: specs/edexcel/computer-science-1CP1.md, Paper 1 and Paper 2 assessment overviews — Paper 1 assesses Topics 1 to 5; Paper 2 is onscreen, 2 hours, 75 marks, six compulsory questions
findings.ruling: NOTE: written-paper command words on onscreen-paper content - relabel in the question-type sweep; rebuild as code-writing tasks only on a unit rebuild.

findings.claim: The simplified postcode check requires code[0] AND code[1] to be alphabetic.
findings.truth: That rejects genuine postcodes with a single leading letter, such as M1 1AA or L1 8JQ (verified: is_valid_postcode('M11AA') returns False). The lesson labels the check “simplified”, so it is defensible teaching code and not worth an edit.

findings.claim: Question 6 requires the difference between validation and verification.
findings.truth: Verification is not named anywhere in Topic 6 of this specification, which lists validation checks only. The content taught about it is correct, so it is harmless extra background rather than an error.

summary: Every Python example, trace table, slice, integer division, modulus and answer key in the unit was re-run in Python 3 and all are correct; no code sample would raise an error or print the wrong output. The real errors are a specification classification error (string taught as a fifth primitive data type when the spec lists it as a structured type), an arithmetic-operator miscount, a postcode length range that contradicts the code beneath it, an ambiguous knowledge check where -1 is also correct, and seven fabricated examiner or mark-scheme claims across four lessons.
